title: The Cellar of Old Chapel Road
premise: Folklorist Ivo Nystrom inherited their aunt's house on Old Chapel Road along with her unfinished field recordings of village songs no one will sing twice. When every mirror in the house begins reflecting the room one second late, the delay widens until Ivo is pulled through into a drowned, echoing version of 1974, where their aunt made a bargain: she took a song — and a child's name — that belonged to something beneath the chapel cellar. Guided by the recordings and by Wren, a villager whose grandmother vanished that year, Ivo must return what was taken before the lag swallows them whole. In the end Ivo gives back the song at terrible cost to their own memories of their aunt, sealing the cellar but leaving the house to Wren, who is left holding the only recording of who Ivo used to be.
about_author: Jude Crane is the pen name of a former archivist who spent years cataloguing oral histories in coastal villages where certain songs were politely never requested twice. They write horror about inheritance, houses that remember, and the debts families leave in attics.

chapters.title: The House That Counts Backwards
chapters.summary: Ivo's POV. Arriving at the inherited house on Old Chapel Road for the estate clearance, Ivo catalogs their aunt Edith's belongings, including a locked reel-to-reel recorder and forty unlabeled tapes. The emotional beat is grief braided with resentment at a woman they barely knew.

chapters.title: Songs No One Sings Twice
chapters.summary: Ivo's POV. Interviewing villagers for a folklore archive, Ivo notices a pattern: everyone sings each song once, then goes pale and changes the subject. Old Tam warns them off 'the cellar ones.' The beat is unease disguised as academic curiosity.

chapters.title: One Second Late
chapters.summary: Ivo's POV. At midnight, Ivo catches their reflection blinking after they do. Testing every mirror in the house, they confirm each one lags exactly one second behind reality. The beat is rationalization cracking under evidence.

chapters.title: Edith's Margins
chapters.summary: Ivo's POV. Reading Edith's field notebooks, Ivo finds her final entries devolving from notation into frantic repetition: 'it keeps the time it is owed.' A tape labeled 1974 plays a child singing a song backwards. The beat is dread deepening into obsession.

chapters.title: Wren
chapters.summary: Ivo's POV, introducing Wren. Wren Halloran, granddaughter of a woman who vanished in 1974, confronts Ivo about removing tapes from the village. Their hostility sparks into reluctant alliance when Wren admits she hears the lag too. The beat is friction becoming connection.

chapters.title: The Chapel Cellar
chapters.summary: Ivo and Wren alternate POV. They explore the flooded cellar beneath the ruined chapel next door, finding a bricked alcove scratched with tally marks — thousands of them, still being added. The beat is claustrophobic discovery.

chapters.title: What Edith Took
chapters.summary: Ivo's POV. A hidden letter reveals Edith recorded the 'cellar song' against explicit warning, and something below demanded payment; she gave it a name instead of herself — Wren's grandmother's name. The beat is horrified understanding.

chapters.title: Two Seconds
chapters.summary: Ivo's POV. The mirror lag doubles overnight. Ivo watches themselves pour tea two seconds behind, and realizes the delay is widening toward something. Wren arrives soaked, saying the river ran uphill past her window. The beat is accelerating wrongness.

chapters.title: The Village Remembers Differently
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Wren canvasses elders and finds their memories of 1974 are mutually contradictory, as if the year has been edited. Only the songs remain consistent — and only when sung once. The beat is grief over a stolen history.

chapters.title: Playback
chapters.summary: Ivo's POV. Playing Edith's 1974 tape fully, Ivo hears beneath the reversed song a second voice answering — patient, enormous, counting. The mirrors all show the room empty except for a figure standing where Ivo stands. The beat is terror of being already claimed.

chapters.title: Love Against Duty
chapters.summary: Dual POV. Wren begs Ivo to burn the tapes and walk away; Ivo refuses, unable to abandon Edith's debt or Wren's grandmother. Their argument becomes a confession of how much they've come to mean to each other. The beat is love declared in the shadow of sacrifice.

chapters.title: Four Seconds
chapters.summary: Ivo's POV. The lag reaches four seconds; Ivo now sees themselves living slightly in the past, eating meals they've already finished. Time around the house moves like tide. The beat is the body rebelling against borrowed minutes.

chapters.title: The Tally Stops
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. The scratches in the cellar alcove have stopped mid-stroke. Whatever counted down has finished waiting. That night every clock in the village reads 3:14 and will not be corrected. The beat is the quiet before the breach.

chapters.title: Through the Glass
chapters.summary: Ivo's POV. The lag closes to zero and snaps — Ivo is pulled through the hallway mirror into the drowned echo of 1974, a silvered version of the house where sound arrives before its cause. The beat is vertigo and severance from the known world.

chapters.title: The Year That Was Kept
chapters.summary: Ivo's POV inside the echo. Ivo navigates a preserved 1974 populated by reflections of villagers, including a young Edith who does not recognize them. Somewhere here, Wren's grandmother waits, unaged. The beat is sorrowful wonder.

chapters.title: The Thing Beneath the Chapel
chapters.summary: Ivo's POV. In the mirrored cellar, Ivo meets what Edith bargained with: not a monster but a ledger, a presence that keeps time owed and names held. It offers a trade — the song returned, or a name given freely. The beat is negotiation with something that cannot lie but cannot forgive.

chapters.title: Wren on the Other Side
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. In the real world, Wren finds Ivo's body motionless before the mirror and the lag reversing — pulling things out instead of in. She sings the cellar song once, deliberately, as an offering to open the way. The beat is courage chosen over safety.

chapters.title: The Price of Returning
chapters.summary: Ivo's POV. To bring back Wren's grandmother's name — freeing her — Ivo must surrender their own memories of Edith: twelve years of telling themselves stories, all of it collateral. Ivo agrees. The beat is love measured against identity.

chapters.title: Given Back
chapters.summary: Climax, dual POV. In the cellar between worlds, Ivo returns the song note by note while Wren holds the mirror open from outside. The thing beneath accepts; the echo collapses; the grandmother's name dissolves into rest. Ivo wakes on the kitchen floor remembering nothing of Edith at all. The beat is catharsis through loss.

chapters.title: Aftermath: The Quiet House
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. The mirrors reflect honestly again. Wren cares for a convalescing Ivo, who looks at her with polite unfamiliarity layered over something warmer. The village's clocks resume, all set to 3:15. The beat is tender disorientation.

chapters.title: What the Recording Holds
chapters.summary: Dual POV. Wren plays Ivo the last tape: Edith's voice thanking whoever finishes her work, followed by Ivo's own younger voice describing why memory matters more than keeping it. Ivo weeps without knowing why. The beat is grief recovered secondhand.

chapters.title: Old Chapel Road, Sung Once
chapters.summary: Epilogue, dual POV. Months later, Ivo and Wren live in the house together; Ivo begins new fieldwork, and at the village festival they sing the cellar song — once, together, freely given. In the clean mirror at home, nothing lags. The beat is hard-won peace, watched over by everything that remembers for them.
